paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In many cities, the last part of a delivery is the slowest and the most expensive. A parcel may cross a country overnight by lorry or train, only to spend much of the next morning in a van that is stuck in traffic or circling a block in search of somewhere to stop. Delivery companies call this final stage the 'last mile', even though the distance involved is often much shorter than that. Because it involves many small stops rather than one long journey, it uses a large share of the driver's time and of the company's fuel. In recent years, a growing number of businesses have tried to solve this problem with an old idea: the cargo bike.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A cargo bike is a bicycle built to carry goods rather than just a rider. Some have a large box mounted in front of the rider, between two wheels; others carry their load on a long frame behind the seat, or pull a separate trailer. Designs like these are not new. Bakers, postal workers and shopkeepers in many countries relied on them long before motor vans became common, and in some places they never disappeared. What has changed is the addition of a small electric motor, which helps the rider when starting from a standstill or climbing a slope. With this assistance, a rider can carry a heavy load across a city without arriving exhausted.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The main advantage of the cargo bike is its size. It can use cycle lanes when roads are blocked, pass through narrow streets where a van cannot fit, and stop directly outside a customer's door instead of in a loading area some distance away. Riders often say that finding a place to park, which can take a van driver several minutes at every stop, is hardly a problem for them at all. Over a full working day, these minutes add up, and in crowded city centres a bike may complete a round of deliveries as quickly as a van, or even more quickly.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There are other benefits too. Cargo bikes do not burn fuel, so they produce no exhaust in the streets where they operate, and the electric versions need only a small battery that can be charged overnight. They are also much quieter than motor vehicles, which matters in residential areas early in the morning. For the companies that use them, the bikes are cheaper to buy and to maintain than vans, and in many cities riders do not need a driving licence. Some local councils have welcomed them for these reasons and have created loading spaces reserved for bikes.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: However, cargo bikes cannot do everything. Their load is limited, so large or very heavy items, such as furniture, still have to travel by van. Their usefulness also depends on the distance between the depot and the customers, since a rider who has to return frequently to collect more parcels loses much of the time saved on the road. To deal with this, some companies have set up small depots, sometimes called micro-hubs, close to the neighbourhoods they serve. A lorry brings goods to the hub early in the day, and the bikes make the final deliveries from there. Finding affordable space for such hubs in a busy city centre, however, can be difficult.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Riders themselves point to another limitation: the weather. Strong wind, heavy rain and icy roads make the work harder and, at times, unsafe, and not every rider is willing to work outdoors in all seasons. Hilly cities present a further challenge, although electric assistance has reduced it. For these reasons, few people expect cargo bikes to replace vans completely. A more likely future is one in which the two work side by side, with vans carrying heavy goods to the edge of the busiest areas and bikes taking care of the rest.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year, many species of birds travel between the places where they breed and the places where they spend the winter. Some cover distances that would challenge a small aircraft, crossing seas, deserts and mountain ranges, and many return not only to the same region but to the same wood or even the same nest. For centuries, people have wondered how they manage this. The answer, as researchers have gradually discovered, is not a single sense but a combination of several, each of which can take over when another is unavailable.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most obvious guide is the sun. Birds that migrate by day appear to use its position to keep a steady direction. This is not as simple as it sounds, because the sun moves across the sky during the day; a bird that simply flew towards it would travel in a curve. Experiments with caged birds have shown that they compensate for this movement using an internal clock. When that clock is shifted, by keeping birds under artificial light at unusual hours, the birds choose the wrong direction by a predictable amount, which suggests that timing is built into the way they read the sun.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Many songbirds, however, travel at night, and for them the stars are more useful. Young birds do not seem to be born knowing particular constellations. Instead, they learn which part of the sky stays still while the rest of the stars turn around it, and they treat that point as north. Researchers have tested this by raising birds under an artificial night sky made to rotate around a different star: as adults, the birds treated the new centre of rotation as north. The finding suggests that what is inherited is the ability to learn, rather than a fixed map.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Neither the sun nor the stars is visible on a cloudy day or night, yet birds are still able to hold their course under thick cloud. One explanation is that they can sense the Earth's magnetic field. This field varies in strength and angle from place to place, and birds appear to use it both as a compass and, possibly, as a rough indication of position. Exactly how they detect it is still debated. Some scientists believe the sense depends on chemical reactions in the eye, while others have looked for tiny magnetic particles in the head, and the two explanations may not exclude each other.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Closer to the end of a journey, other senses become important. Many birds recognise coastlines, rivers and mountain ridges, and some appear to follow them even when a more direct route is available. Seabirds that spend months over open water face a different problem, as the ocean offers few visible landmarks. There is growing evidence that some of them rely on smell, detecting chemicals released by plankton in particular areas of the sea and building up a picture of the ocean from the odours carried on the wind.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Experience also plays a part. In several species, young birds making their first journey travel in a fixed direction for a set period, as though following inherited instructions. If they are blown off course, they often continue in the same direction and end up far from the usual wintering grounds. Adult birds that are moved in the same way, by contrast, frequently correct their route. This difference suggests that, over one or more journeys, birds develop a sense of where their destination lies, not only of which direction to fly.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These abilities, refined over a very long time, now face new pressures. Bright lights in cities can confuse birds that migrate at night, drawing them towards buildings, and changes in climate are shifting the timing of the seasons on which migration depends. Understanding how birds navigate is therefore not only a scientific puzzle but also a practical concern, since it helps to explain why some journeys are becoming more dangerous and what might be done to make them safer.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Nobody enjoys waiting. Whether it takes place at a bank counter, at a passport desk or on the telephone while recorded music plays, time spent waiting tends to feel longer than the same amount of time spent doing almost anything else. For organisations that serve the public, this creates a difficult problem. Reducing the length of a wait usually means hiring more staff or opening more counters, both of which are expensive. Yet researchers who study the experience of waiting have argued that its length is only part of the story. How long a wait feels, and how it is remembered afterwards, depends on a range of factors that have little to do with the clock.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first of these concerns what people are doing while they wait. Unoccupied time appears to pass more slowly than time that is filled with activity, even when the activity is trivial. A story frequently repeated in discussions of this subject concerns an office building whose tenants complained about slow lifts. Rather than replace the lifts, the owners are said to have installed mirrors beside them, and the complaints stopped, apparently because people now had something to look at. Whether or not the story is accurate in every detail, the principle behind it is widely applied: waiting areas offer magazines, screens and windows, and restaurants hand menus to customers who have not yet been seated.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second factor is uncertainty. A wait of unknown length is generally experienced as longer and more stressful than a wait whose end is known, even if the two last for the same time. This is one reason why many transport systems now display the minutes remaining until the next train or bus. The information does not make the vehicle arrive any sooner, but it allows passengers to decide how to use the time, and it removes the anxiety of wondering whether they have been forgotten. Closely related is the value of explanation: people tend to accept a delay more calmly when they are told why it has happened than when it is left unexplained.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Perhaps the strongest influence of all is the sense of fairness. People who see others served before them, despite having arrived later, often become angry, even if their own wait has hardly been affected. For this reason, many banks and post offices have replaced a set of separate lines, one for each counter, with a single winding line that feeds all the counters in turn. Studies of such systems suggest that the average wait is not necessarily shorter. What changes is that customers no longer watch a neighbouring line move faster than their own, and the feeling that the system is fair makes the wait easier to bear.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The value of what lies at the end of a wait also matters. People are prepared to wait far longer for something they consider important, such as medical treatment or a ticket to a rare event, than for something routine. Waiting alone, too, seems to feel longer than waiting with others, perhaps because company provides both distraction and reassurance. Taken together, these observations suggest that a wait is less a fixed quantity of time than an experience shaped by expectation and circumstance.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: There is also evidence that the way a wait ends has a disproportionate effect on how it is later remembered. When people recall an unpleasant experience, they seem to give particular weight to its final moments. A wait that finishes with a friendly greeting and quick service may therefore be remembered more favourably than a shorter wait that ends with a curt refusal. For organisations, this suggests that improving the last few minutes of an experience can be as valuable as shortening its overall length.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is comfortable with these findings. Critics point out that techniques for making a wait feel shorter can easily become a way of avoiding the real cost of reducing it. A screen in a waiting room, they argue, is no substitute for an adequate number of staff, and an organisation that relies on such methods may simply be managing complaints rather than improving its service. Supporters reply that the two approaches are not alternatives: even the most efficient system will sometimes involve waiting, and when it does, there is no reason why the experience should be worse than it needs to be.
